text.title: AI Pre-Screen Bias Guardrails Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every AI-assisted hiring pre-screen or take-home review MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Before any model reads a CV, cover letter or take-home, a separate redaction step MUST remove: name, photo, email handle, date of birth and age, graduation years, address below city level, gender markers and pronouns, nationality and visa status, marital and parental status, and any club, church or association that reveals a protected class. The redaction function is unit-tested on a fixture set, and a sample of redacted documents is inspected by a human at every release.

rationale.source: Bertrand and Mullainathan 2004, 'Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal?'; Goldin and Rouse 2000 on blind orchestra auditions

rule.rationale: Identical CVs with different names receive materially different callback rates from human screeners, and models trained on human-labelled hiring data reproduce the same pattern. The model cannot be told to ignore a name; the only reliable control is that it never sees one.

rule.statement: The scoring rubric MUST be written, versioned and hashed before the first candidate is scored. Every criterion maps to a stated job requirement and carries behavioural anchors for at least the lowest, middle and highest score. The rubric version is recorded on every score; a rubric change re-runs calibration (see `r-calibration-sample-before-go-live`).

rationale.source: Schmidt and Hunter 1998, 'The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology'; structured-interview research

rule.rationale: Unstructured judgement is the least predictive and most bias-prone selection method in the literature; structure is what carries validity. A rubric written after the scores exist is a rationalisation, and a criterion with no anchor lets the model invent its own scale per candidate.

rule.statement: The rubric and the prompt MUST NOT ask for or reward: "culture fit", "energy", "polish", "native speaker", "recent graduate", "digital native", employment gaps, years since graduation, commute distance, or the prestige of a school or employer. The criterion list is reviewed against this proxy list at every rubric change, and the review is recorded in `evidence[]`.

rationale.source: EEOC technical assistance, May 2023, 'Select Issues: Assessing Adverse Impact in Software, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence Used in Employment Selection Procedures Under Title VII'

rule.rationale: A criterion does not need to name a protected class to select on one: employment gaps track parental leave and disability, "native speaker" tracks national origin, "recent graduate" tracks age. Disparate impact through a proxy carries the same liability as direct discrimination.

rule.statement: Before go-live, and after every change to the prompt, rubric, model id or redaction step, a calibration sample drawn from the real applicant pool MUST be scored blind by at least two human reviewers and by the system. The agreement statistic (Cohen's kappa, weighted kappa or Spearman rank correlation), its numeric acceptance threshold set in advance, and the run URL go in `evidence[]`. Below threshold, the system does not score candidates.

rationale.source: Inter-rater reliability practice in personnel assessment; widely established practice in ML validation

rule.rationale: A model that agrees with reviewers on synthetic CVs and disagrees on real ones is measuring the synthetic distribution. Without a pre-set threshold the team decides after seeing the number whether it was good enough, which is exactly the judgement the calibration was meant to replace.

rule.statement: At every stage where the system filters or ranks, pass-through rates MUST be computed per protected group from self-identification data held separately from the scoring pipeline. A selection rate for any group below four-fifths (80%) of the highest group's rate puts the system on hold and opens a review; the per-stage table is attached to every review cycle.

rationale.source: EEOC Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, 29 CFR 1607.4(D)

rule.rationale: The four-fifths rule is the enforcement agencies' stated threshold for adverse impact, and it can only be checked with group counts per stage. A team that never computes the ratio discovers the disparity when a regulator or plaintiff computes it for them, over the full history of the system.

rule.statement: The system MUST NOT reject, advance or rank-out a candidate on its own. Its output is a score with rubric-referenced reasons; every advance or reject record carries the `role:handle` of the human of record who made the decision, and that human has the redacted document and the score in front of them, not the score alone.

rationale.source: GDPR Art. 22 (decisions based solely on automated processing); EU AI Act Annex III (recruitment and selection as high-risk); NYC Local Law 144 of 2021

rule.rationale: A score threshold that auto-rejects is a solely automated decision with legal effect, which the GDPR lets the candidate contest and the EU AI Act regulates as high-risk. The human of record is also the only mechanism that catches the redaction miss or rubric bug on a single candidate before it becomes a pattern.

rule.statement: Where the role is subject to an automated-employment-decision-tool law, the guardrail spec MUST link the candidate notice text and the most recent independent bias audit in `evidence[]`. For NYC Local Law 144 that means notice at least 10 business days before the tool is used and a bias audit conducted within the preceding year, with its summary published. For other jurisdictions, record which law applies or an explicit "none applies" with the counsel who confirmed it.

rationale.source: NYC Local Law 144 of 2021 and its DCWP implementing rules (6 RCNY 5-300 et seq.)

rule.rationale: The notice and audit obligations attach to the employer, not the vendor, and they attach per role and per jurisdiction of the candidate. A spec that does not say which law applies has not been checked by legal, whatever the DEI review concluded.

rule.statement: For every candidate scored, the pipeline MUST retain: the hash of the original submission, the redacted text as sent to the model, the model id, prompt hash and rubric version, the score with reasons, and the human of record's decision. Retention MUST be at least the applicable record-keeping period (29 CFR 1602.14 sets one year for most private US employers; check the jurisdiction) and the log is queryable per candidate on request.

rationale.source: EEOC record-keeping regulation 29 CFR 1602.14; GDPR Art. 15 right of access

rule.rationale: A candidate's challenge, a regulator's request or an internal four-fifths investigation all reduce to one question: what exactly did the system see and say for this person? If the redacted text and the rubric version were not stored, the answer is a reconstruction, and reconstructions do not survive discovery.
